The texts tie the timing to the renouncer's qualification: in due order for most, at once for one of intense dispassion; and the Maitreya distinguishes outer ritual renunciation from inner renunciation.
The Nirālamba itself places caste in convention (vyavahāra) and the true brāhmaṇa at the level of realized truth, so both can hold on different levels.
Both sides also read the staff inwardly (three restraints; staff of knowledge), and the Advaitin texts grade marks by kind of renouncer, but the Śāṭyāyanīya binds all kinds to the marks.
The Śāṇḍilya names two ways of ending mind — yoga and knowledge — suited to different people, and the Varāha's bird and ant paths both reach Brahman.

The Yogaśikhā itself distinguishes contrived powers (from substances, rites, mantras — impermanent) from spontaneous ones (arising in those free of vāsanās); the former are obstacles, the latter signs.

Both texts assign outer forms to worshippers and inner worship to renouncers and knowers: the Rāmapūrvatāpanī says forms are 'for the sake of worshippers', the Maitreya restricts its rule to the seeker of liberation.
The identity Upaniṣads read the names as one reality (Viṣṇu the heart of Śiva, Śiva of Viṣṇu), and each sectarian text's supremacy claim can be read as praise of the chosen deity.
The prohibitions bind the renouncer on the way; the Avadhūta speaks of the one whose work is done, and the Sannyāsa's rule itself exempts disciples taken out of compassion.
Not yet reconciled: the restrictive lists govern ritual renunciation, the open statements define the renouncer by inner dispassion; whether one limits the other is not settled here.

The fifteen limbs read as knowledge, and the list of obstacles in samādhi, shared between the Aparokṣānubhūti and the Tejobindu.

The critique of birth-caste under the title 'Vajrasūcī' ('diamond needle'): a Buddhist Vajrasūcī (attributed to Aśvaghoṣa; in Chinese to Dharmakīrti) and the Vajrasūci Upaniṣad share title and line of argument.
The sixteen names of the Kalisantaraṇa, recited in Gauḍīya practice as the mahāmantra (usually with the 'hare kṛṣṇa' half first).

The renunciation rite (praiṣa, virajā homa, abandonment of topknot and thread), the kinds of renouncer, the paramahaṃsa ideal and the giving of the great saying at initiation; the four seats of the Maṭhāmnāya.
Triple-staff renunciation keeping topknot and thread (Śāṭyāyanīya), codified in Yādavaprakāśa's Yatidharmasamuccaya and followed by Śrīvaiṣṇava ascetics.
Śrīvidyā mantra, cakra, nityās and inner worship in the Tripurā, Tripurātāpanī, Bhāvanā and Bahvṛca; Śrīvidyā commentators (Bhāskararāya) in turn cite these Upaniṣads as śruti.
The vyūha deities (Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha) in the Triśikhi's element concentrations and the Mudgala's account of Aniruddha.
The Darśana Upaniṣad's ten yamas and niyamas, channels, inner tīrthas and five withdrawals parallel the Yoga Yājñavalkya.
